newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone bank reopens doors after May 25 coup.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone bank reopens doors after May 25 coup.

text.p: State-owned Sierre Leone Commercial Bank reopened its doors on Wednesday for the first time since a coup on May 25 after the new military government said it would guarantee its safety.
"The government has, after repeated meetings with them, convinced us that they will protect us and our operations fully," a senior official at the bank said.
Other banks, including foreign banks, in the capital, Freetown, remain closed.
The Commercial Bank official said the government had also "assured us of other technical issues, such as the matter of liquidity, in case we run across such a problem".
He said that the bank was giving priority to corporate customers who needed large sums of money to pay staff who had not received their wages for two months.
Customers were waiting in two long queues when the bank opened its doors on Wednesday morning. Heavily armed police were posted around the building.
Joseph Cole, a 50-year-old public sector worker, said his family had run out of food and he wanted to get money from a savings account to buy something to eat.
Another man, a motor mechanic, said he would withdraw all he could in order to take his family to safety in Conakry, the capital of neighbouring Guinea.
A large hole remained in the yellow glass of the ground-floor window, a reminder of the coup that brought Major Johnny Paul Koroma to power.

Other countries grouped within the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) are putting pressure on the army leaders to restore ousted President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, and could use force if diplomatic efforts fail.
Trade unions have been told that other banks in Freetown and the rest of the country will remain closed for now.

"The parent companies of Barclays and Standard Chartered have written to the Sierra Leone Labour Congress that their banks will remain shut for the time being, despite calls by the present military government to reopen them, until the security situation improves considerably," a union leader said.

"Our case is different from the foreign-owned banks," said the Sierra Leone Commercial Bank official. "We are mainly owned and run by the government and, whatever happens, we are bound to comply with government orders."
